t: Do You Ever Feel Coldhearted Enforcing Consequences? ences/
q: But letting students off the hook is a mistake. It’s a mistake every time .

A second chance is already built into the classroom management plan we recommend here at SCM. Its purpose is to give students an opportunity to take care of it on their own and without a true consequence.
Each time you go back on your word and fail to do what you promised—in this case, following your plan as it’s written—your students will trust you less and less.
Children have an acute sense of fairness. So when they see you letting some students off the hook and not others—regardless of your reasoning—they’ll resent you.
The truth is, though it may sometimes feel like it, it isn’t coldhearted. Rather, it’s an act of compassion to care enough about your students to make the tough decisions.
You’ll have proven once again that you mean what you say, that you’re a person of your word, and that you can be trusted.

t: 3 Ways You Should Never Vent About Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/12/05/3-ways-you-should-never-vent-about-students/
q: Unless you’re taking part in a professional conversation that you could or would document, you should never mention the student by name—even if it’s obvious who the student is.

When venting, keep the focus on you and your frustrations. Vent about your feelings. It’s fine to express disappointment and irritation, even anger, but avoid complaining about any student personally.
And no matter how hard you try, it’s something you can’t hide. Your dislike will reveal itself in subtle but sure ways that the student will pick up on.
It’s all too common to overhear teachers in hallways, offices, and staff lounges complaining about students by name and without a care in the world who hears them.
Teachers who openly complain about students aren’t well respected. They’re secretly avoided by most staff members.
It’s healthy when your first priority is to protect the dignity of every student in your class.
x: Venting to trusted colleagues about your own frustrations is healthy, but venting about specific students by name carries real risk.
Verbalizing personal dislike for a student solidifies that feeling and will eventually surface in how you treat them.

Complaining about students in hallways, offices, or lounges risks being overheard by parents or volunteers and fueling rumors.
Teachers who openly and chronically complain about students are less respected and rarely take responsibility for improving.
Healthy venting protects student dignity, focuses on your own feelings, and happens only with someone you deeply trust.
